events.title: Learning Seminar in Algebraic Combinatorics
events.summary: Attend a mathematics seminar discussing torus-equivariant cohomology classes of smooth projective varieties. The session will explore the 6-vertex model and its relation to computing products of Schubert classes for flag varieties.

evidence.description: Torus-equivariant cohomology classes of smooth projective varieties (e.g. flag varieties) are determined by their restrictions to fixed points. We'll compute these for Schubert classes in type A, using the 5-vertex model and colored extensions. The 6-vertex will be about the "Chern-Schwartz-MacPherson" deformations of Schubert classes. Then we'll introduce a trivalent analogue of R-matrices and use it to compute the products of Schubert classes, for up to 4-step flag varieties.

events.title: The Tree of Eternity
events.summary: The Tree of Eternity is an immersive, interactive installation that explores remembrance, loss, and the enduring presence of those we have loved. The installation centers on a projected tree surrounded by interactive terminal pods that control its structure. Visitors approach interactive pods positioned throughout the gallery space, where they are invited to recall memories of people or experiences throughout their lives. Depending on the kiosk they interact with, different effects will be present on the projected tree. As more visitors’ memories are inputted, the tree’s visuals adapt and change form, demonstrating that our memories persist with us. Projection mapping creates ethereal visuals accompanied by atmospheric audio. Even when visitors aren't actively engaging with the kiosks, the system generates ambient transmissions, suggesting that the tree—and the memories it embodies—continues to live and grow. The installation creates a dialogue between life and death, presence and absence, individual memory and collective remembrance, inviting participants to contribute to a living memorial that persists beyond any single moment of grief or reflection.

events.summary: University Carillonist Tiffany Ng performs on the Charles Baird Carillon, an instrument of 53 bronze bells located inside the Burton Memorial Tower. The largest bell, which strikes the hour, weighs 12 tons, while the smallest bell, 4½ octaves above, weighs just 15 pounds. Thirty-minute recitals are performed on the Charles Baird Carillon at noon every weekday that classes are in session, followed by visitor Q&A with the carillonist. The bell chamber may be accessed via a combination of elevator and stairs. Take the elevator to the highest floor possible (floor 8), and then climb two flights of stairs (39 steps) to the bell chamber (floor 10). Hearing protection earmuffs are provided for visitors. Be prepared to walk on ice and snow in the bell chamber during winter. Built in 1936, the Charles Baird Carillon is not ADA accessible. Visitors with mobility concerns are invited to visit the Lurie Carillon.

events.experienceId: experience:["ann arbor","walgreen drama center","ncks colloquium series dying tree embodying jungyong in contemporary korean choreography"]
events.title: NCKS Colloquium Series | Dying Tree: Embodying Jungyong in Contemporary Korean Choreography
events.summary: Attend in person or via Zoom at https://myumi.ch/J45y2 Synopsis: Dying Tree is an original movement practice developed by choreographer Kim Jaeduk through improvisation and close observation of the body. Inspired by his reflections on Jungyong (中庸), a philosophical concept rooted in Confucian thought, this practice explores how movement can be sustained and transformed aesthetically through the interplay of force and balance, speed and expression. This colloquium takes as its starting point an image that emerged from observing Kim Jaeduk's improvisational movement: a body that appears almost motionless, like a dying tree in winter, while an intense flow of energy continues within. This contrast between outward stillness and inner vitality connects to a longstanding question in Kim Jaeduk's choreographic practice: how can movement be sustained through continuous change? The image became a point of departure for developing the physical principles of Dying Tree and gradually shaping them into a distinct movement style. The presentation explores how the concept of Jungyong is embodied through several key movement principles. These include Chumi (醜美), which explores asymmetrical bodily forms and the aesthetic potential of unconventional shapes; Jwause (左右勢), which organizes lateral shifts and changes in the body's center; and Changyeong (贊輕), which cultivates a deliberately light quality of movement. The presentation also examines the relationship between Hyeongsik(形式), the structural organization of movement that can be physically learned and repeated, and Hyeongyong (形容), which expands its expressive possibilities. Through this relationship, it considers how established movement structures can become the basis for new choreographic expressions. Combining a spoken presentation with live movement demonstrations, the colloquium shows how philosophical ideas can inform physical exploration, movement training, and the creative process of contemporary choreography. Rather than presenting Dying Tree as a direct representation of a particular philosophical tradition, this colloquium approaches it as an ongoing artistic practice through which ideas are interpreted, tested, and explored through the body. From Kim Jaeduk's choreographic perspective, it seeks to illuminate how embodied knowledge, philosophical inquiry, and creative experimentation intersect in the making of contemporary dance. Biography: Kim Jae-duk is an internationally acclaimed South Korean choreographer and composer, currently serving as the Artistic Director of Modern Table Contemporary Dance Company in Korea and Resident Choreographer of T.H.E Dance Company in Singapore. Recognized for his distinctive choreographic language, Kim creates dynamic works that bring together contemporary dance, music, rhythm, and physical expression. His artistic practice explores the relationship between movement and sound, drawing inspiration from diverse cultural influences and traditional rhythmic structures to develop a unique and powerful performance vocabulary. Kim has established an extensive international presence through commissions and collaborations with leading dance companies across Asia, Europe, Oceania, and South America. His choreographic works have been presented by institutions including the Argentine National Contemporary Dance Company, Lucerne Municipal Dance Company TanzLuzern in Switzerland, Hong Kong City Contemporary Dance Company (CCDC), New Zealand Dance Company, Curitiba Municipal Ballet in Brazil, and the Seoul Metropolitan Dance Theatre. His notable works include Tension Espacial, commissioned by the Argentine National Contemporary Dance Company in 2015 and subsequently revived for a total of 48 performances in 2026; Jangdan, created for Hong Kong CCDC; Brown, which received three awards at the 2023 Hong Kong Dance Awards; JE-UI, commissioned by TanzLuzern; and MEDITA, which received the 2025 Grand Prize in Choreography from the Korean Association of Dance Critics. His work Sokdowas also selected for the official showcase of Tanzmesse in Germany in 2020. In recognition of his outstanding artistic achievements, Kim received the 2024 New York Bessie Award for Outstanding Choreography. His other accolades include the Korea Modern Dance Association's Choreographer of the Year Award, three awards at the 24th Hong Kong Dance Awards in 2023 for Brown, the Music & Sound Design Award at the 21st Hong Kong Dance Awards in 2019 for Jangdan, and a Commendation from the Minister of Culture, Sports and Tourism of Korea in 2018. Beyond his choreographic work, Kim is actively involved in international artistic exchange and education. He has led workshops and participated in residency and educational programmes at major international platforms, including ImPulsTanz – Vienna International Dance Festival and the Centre National de la Danse (CND) in Paris. In 2008, he was invited to lecture at the Rambert School of Ballet and Contemporary Dance in the United Kingdom. Through his ongoing work in Korea and Singapore, as well as his collaborations with international dance companies and cultural institutions, Kim Jae-duk continues to expand the possibilities of contemporary dance, establishing a distinctive artistic voice on the global stage. *If there is anything we can do to make this event accessible to you, please contact us at namhy@umich.edu. legacySeriesKeys: "don't let the sun": chamber choir & university choir|hill auditorium
events.title: "Don't Let The Sun": Chamber Choir & University Choir
events.summary: WORLD PREMIERE Composer Theodore Wiprud and librettist Richard Wesley have created an oratorio examining a widespread expression of racism in America, documented in the landmark book *Sundown Towns* by the late sociologist and historian James Loewen. Conducted by Director of University Choirs Eugene Rogers, *Don’t Let the Sun*, for chorus, vocal soloists, and orchestra, will run approximately 90 minutes (plus intermission). It tells the story of “sundown towns” where residents drove out or actively excluded specific groups from residing there (from being in a town after sunset) through ordinances, signs, and acts of violence. Sundown towns excluded Black people, and in some cases, Chinese Americans, Jewish people, Native Americans, Latinas/os and other racialized groups. Since the 19th century these towns have been prevalent throughout the U.S. and especially in the Midwest, West, and East. These policies did not completely disappear over time. The attitudes that drove them morphed into housing “covenants,” redlining, discrimination within the post-war FHA and discrimination in the granting of bank loans. The results of these decisions and policies haunt our country to this very day. *Don’t Let the Sun* will shine a light on this difficult chapter in America’s ever-expanding history, and help audiences engage productively with “hard” histories. Mr. Loewen’s *Sundown Towns: A Hidden Dimension of American Racism* is the definitive history of these phenomena. Another source is the “History and Social Justice” website launched by Dr. Loewen, which has had nearly one million visitors over the last three years, and continues to amass cases and first-hand accounts. Librettist Richard Wesley’s text is inspired by the voices of individuals impacted by sundown towns and more recent policies, examining the harm experienced by both the excluded and the excluders; and recent efforts by many sundown towns to reckon with their past and shape a better future. CONTENT ADVISORY: This program explores the difficult history of sundown towns in America, including themes of racial discrimination, antisemitism, exclusion, and historical language that some audience members may find disturbing. POST-CONCERT DISCUSSION: Composer Theodore Wiprud will join a discussion on stage directly following the concert. (The post-concert discussion will not be livestreamed.) *"Don't Let the Sun" was commissioned with support from an Arts Initiative Project Support (AIPS) grant, an Arts Research: Incubation and Acceleration (ARIA) grant, the U-M Brehm Choral Commissioning Fund and generous support from the Department of History, the Department of American Culture, and the School of Music, Theatre & Dance.* ––– *Parking / Traffic alert for attendees:* https://smtd.umich.edu/2026-construction ABOUT THE GUEST ARTISTS THEODORE WIPRUD is a composer, an educator, and a researcher on the musical community’s work toward equity and inclusion. Many of his works address social issues, including vocal works like *American Journal* (Robert Hayden) and *A Georgia Song* (Maya Angelou); and orchestral works like his Violin Concerto *“Katrina”; Wind of Many Voices*, responding to the troubled history of South Dakota; and a second Violin Concerto *“on the brink”* exploring climate grief and climate action. RICHARD WESLEY is a playwright and screenwriter whose many plays deal with social-historical moments. He wrote the libretto for Anthony Davis’ Pulitzer Prize-winning opera *Central Park Five*. Mr. Wesley has received numerous awards including the NAACP Image Award for Best Picture (for *Uptown Saturday Night*) and the National Black Theater Festival’s August Wilson Playwright Award. He teaches at New York University.

events.title: The Tree of Eternity
events.summary: The Tree of Eternity is an immersive, interactive installation that explores remembrance, loss, and the enduring presence of those we have loved. The installation centers on a projected tree surrounded by interactive terminal pods that control its structure. Visitors approach interactive pods positioned throughout the gallery space, where they are invited to recall memories of people or experiences throughout their lives. Depending on the kiosk they interact with, different effects will be present on the projected tree. As more visitors’ memories are inputted, the tree’s visuals adapt and change form, demonstrating that our memories persist with us. Projection mapping creates ethereal visuals accompanied by atmospheric audio. Even when visitors aren't actively engaging with the kiosks, the system generates ambient transmissions, suggesting that the tree—and the memories it embodies—continues to live and grow. The installation creates a dialogue between life and death, presence and absence, individual memory and collective remembrance, inviting participants to contribute to a living memorial that persists beyond any single moment of grief or reflection.

events.title: Awakening the Dragon–Showcasing the Building and Performance of an Asian Icon
events.summary: Experience a curated experience of the imaginary, featuring a lightly sci-fi, magnificent work of art--the LRCCS Fortune and Longevity Dragon, a 25-ft long, Asian-inspired full-body dragon sculpture for use in the traditional "dragon dance" crafted by renowned international artist Zhen Guo with U-M faculty arts lecturer Raymond Wetzel, artist Jeri Rosenberg, students, and volunteers The exhibition highlights the story of the dragon's fabrication and its impact on community.. An iconic symbol of inclusivity, strength, and courage, this newly imagined U-M dragon, with its futuristic flair, technological creativity and sustainable materials, invites students and the entire community to re-envision a classic cultural symbol for contemporary times. Presented by the Lieberthal-Rogel Center for Chinese Studies. This project was made possible by grants from the University of Michigan Arts Initiative and the Office of the Provost, Global Engagement. Additional funding was provided by ArtsEngine, Center for World Performance Studies, Stearns Collection of Musical Instruments, and U.S. Department of Education. events.title: THEATRE l She Kills Monsters
events.summary: Planet Ant Theatre presents SHE KILLS MONSTERS by Qui Nguyen, December 4-19, 2026, at Ant Hall. When Agnes Evans loses her teenage sister Tilly, she realizes she barely knew her. Tilly's Dungeons & Dragons notebook pulls Agnes into a fantastical world of epic quests, homicidal fairies, snarling ogres, and 90s pop culture as she tries to reconnect with her sister and find the courage she never knew she had. Equal parts comedy, heartfelt drama, and action-packed adventure, the play celebrates the power of great storytelling and the geek and warrior in all of us. Content advisory: Strong language, stage combat, sexual references, and themes of grief, bullying, and suicide. Recommended for ages 13+. She Kills Monsters is presented by arrangement with Concord Theatricals on behalf of Samuel French, Inc. For more information, visit www.concordtheatricals.com.

events.title: Stephen Rush presents a Fluxus Concert
events.summary: Professor of Performing Arts Technology Stephen Rush presents an afternoon full of Fluxus events and compositions. Is it theater? Is it music? Is it Art? Come see. The audience will see, hear, and experience *audience-friendly* Fluxus compositions by John Cage, La Monte Young, Yoko Ono, Michael Gould, Ben Patterson, Toshi Ichiyanagi, Matthew Evan Taylor and some compositions – never-before-performed – written by Rush when he was nine years old. featuredEvents.experienceId: experience:["ann arbor","east hall","learning seminar in algebraic combinatorics"]
featuredEvents.title: Learning Seminar in Algebraic Combinatorics
featuredEvents.summary: Attend a mathematics seminar discussing torus-equivariant cohomology classes of smooth projective varieties. The session will explore the 6-vertex model and its relation to computing products of Schubert classes for flag varieties.

evidence.description: Torus-equivariant cohomology classes of smooth projective varieties (e.g. flag varieties) are determined by their restrictions to fixed points. We'll compute these for Schubert classes in type A, using the 5-vertex model and colored extensions. The 6-vertex will be about the "Chern-Schwartz-MacPherson" deformations of Schubert classes. Then we'll introduce a trivalent analogue of R-matrices and use it to compute the products of Schubert classes, for up to 4-step flag varieties.
